::: {.legend}

| Stage | CLI | Skill |
|---|---|---|
| **Capture** | `wt idea "…"` | `wt-capture`, `wt-seed` |
| **Explore** | `wt idea log / summary / questions` | `wt-explore` |
| **Accept spec** | `wt spec new --from-idea` | `wt-new-work`, `wt-rework` |
| **Export (handoff)** | `wt spec export` | `wt-export` |
| **Implement** | — | `wt-implement-spec` *(runs in the owning repo)* |
| **Close the loop** | `wt spec pull-status/pull-clock/fit-log` · `wt idea close` | — |

**🤖 = needs human/AI judgment · ⚙️ = deterministic wt CLI (mechanical, no judgment).** wt's CLI never *decides* anything — every write (state, property, clock entry) is a drift-guarded, idempotent record of a decision already made. Judgment lives entirely in the Skills layer: what to explore, whether a design actually holds up, whether the code is really done, whether it actually worked.

**Triage, anywhere:** `wt hub --json` · `wt next` — read-only, non-mutating.
**Terminal exits are healthy outcomes, not failures:** *dropped* = won't-do, reasoned; *researched* = explored fully, value folded elsewhere via a pointer.
**"Your machine" is not one place** — ideas/Log/Clock live in **org files**, draft specs live in the **wt data dir** (outbox), and export schemes live in **config**; none of this is the wt tool's own source code. Only **implementation** crosses into the **owning repo** — a genuinely different codebase, no shared files, no `wt` CLI. Only three things ever cross that boundary: the spec file going out, and status + time log coming back.

:::
